title: From big goals to game plan: How to prepare for a major purchase.
summary: Thinking about a major purchase? Learn how to review your cash flow, credit, savings, and timeline before exploring home loan options.
body_markdown:
Before any numbers, get specific about what you are actually planning:


-


What you are buying


-


When you hope to buy


-


Whether that timeline can flex


-


What could change between now and then


-


Which costs are one-time and which are ongoing


That last one carries more weight than it looks. A down payment is a single event you can save toward and be done with. Property taxes, insurance, utilities, and maintenance are permanent additions to your monthly life.


Pull the last three months and look honestly at:


-


How consistent your income actually is


-


What you already pay toward existing debt


-


What you currently spend on housing


-


Insurance and taxes


-


Maintenance or ownership expenses you already carry


-


How much monthly flexibility is genuinely left over


If your money is spread across more than one institution, that review is harder than it needs to be. Our[Personal Finance Manager](https://www.axosbank.com/personal/personal-finance-manager) syncs both Axos and non-Axos accounts into a single view and categorizes transactions automatically. It is free to use, no account needed.


Worth knowing: a lender qualifying you and you deciding what you can live with are two different tests. Lenders work from ratios built on documented income and documented debt.


Your actual month includes childcare, the car that needs work, and the flexibility you want to keep. A loan you qualify for and a payment that leaves room to breathe are not automatically the same number, and only one of those tests is run by someone who knows your life (you).


The purchase price is not the bill. Depending on the transaction, you may also encounter a down payment, closing costs, inspections, an appraisal, prepaid taxes or insurance, moving expenses, and the repairs or furnishings that show up in month one.


Closing costs deserve a closer look, because the number moves depending on who is counting.


A 2026 analysis of more than 620,000 purchase quotes put average total closing costs at $4,528, or about 1.04% of the sale price, but that figure counts title, settlement, recording, and transfer taxes only. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's more familiar 2% to 5% range covers the whole closing bill, including lender origination fees and the prepaid escrow the lender collects up front. Both numbers are accurate. They are measuring different things, and the gap between them is roughly threefold. ([Closing cost data study, RealCostIQ, July 2026](https://realcostiq.com/data/closing-costs-by-state/) )


So when someone quotes you a closing cost figure, the first question is not “how much.” It is “which fees are in that number.”


There is a document designed to answer exactly that. Within three business days of your application, a lender is required to send you a Loan Estimate, a standardized form showing your projected closing costs line by line.


Because every lender uses the same format, it is the one genuinely apples-to-apples comparison you will get. ([Loan Estimate explainer, Consumer Financial Protection Bureau](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/loan-estimate/) )


It is worth comparing carefully. The CFPB has reported that median total loan costs rose more than 36% between 2021 and 2023, driven largely by increases in credit report, appraisal, and title service fees. Those are the line items most worth reading twice.


Before you apply anywhere:


-


Review your credit reports from all three bureaus


-


Look for reporting errors and dispute anything wrong


-


Keep payments on time in the months leading up


-


Understand what you currently owe and to whom


-


Avoid taking on new debt you do not need before applying


Two details most people miss. First,[AnnualCreditReport.com](https://www.annualcreditreport.com/) is the only federally authorized source, and all three bureaus have made free weekly access permanent, so there is no reason to check less than a few times before a mortgage application. ([Free credit reports, Federal Trade Commission](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/free-credit-reports) )


Second, those free reports do not include your credit score. The reports are the underlying data; the score is calculated separately by FICO or VantageScore. Checking a score in an app tells you the summary. Reading the reports is how you find any errors.


The two tools work together rather than competing. Pull the reports to find errors; watch a score over time to see the trend. We offer free credit score monitoring through Experian in the Axos app. More on preparing the financial side in[our guide to saving for a house](https://www.axosbank.com/personal/insights/loans/home/saving-for-a-house) .


This is general education rather than individual credit advice. Your situation may call for something different, and a mortgage professional can speak to specifics.


There is a strong temptation to put every available dollar toward the purchase, especially when a larger down payment improves the terms. Resist emptying the reserve entirely.


The cash you need is not the same as the cash due at closing. A new home tends to generate expenses immediately—the thing the inspection flagged, the appliance that fails in month two, the deposit nobody mentioned.


Closing with nothing left turns an ordinary expense into a crisis. Preserving a cushion is not a lack of commitment to the purchase. It is part of the purchase.


Once you are ready to talk to lenders, the quality of your questions determines the quality of your comparison. Ask about:


-


Which loan types you may be eligible for


-


The interest rate, and whether it is fixed or adjustable


-


Every fee, including the lender fee and whether it can be reduced or waived


-


The estimated monthly payment including taxes and insurance


-


What documentation you will need to provide


-


The expected closing timeline


-


Whether refinancing is relevant to your situation


Then get the Loan Estimate from more than one lender and compare them side by side. The rate is the number everyone quotes. The total cost is the number that matters.
